title: SniffKitty Odor Sensor
alt: SniffKitty ESP32-S3 odor-sensing prototype in a red 3D-printed enclosure
summary: An ESP32-S3 multisensor system for pet-space odor monitoring, presence detection, local logging, and a live web dashboard.
role: Firmware, hardware integration, assembly, and enclosure design
focus: Embedded C++, sensors, networking, and rapid prototyping
stack: ESP32-S3 · C++ · MQ135/MQ137 · AHT10 · Camera · microSD · CAD
challenge: Combine analog gas sensors, environmental sensing, camera input, storage, and a web interface in a compact physical prototype.
process: Implemented firmware for sampling and baseline comparison, camera-based presence detection, offline access-point fallback, microSD logging, and status feedback. Built the circuit and designed the 3D-printed enclosure.
outcome: Produced a self-contained prototype with live monitoring, local event capture, resilient storage, and documented hardware variants.
overview: SniffKitty was designed as a private, local-first way to observe relative odor changes around a pet space. The final demo build combines two gas sensors, environmental sensing, camera-based motion detection, local storage, a browser dashboard, and a physical enclosure in one ESP32-S3 system. Six working hardware branches document the path from the first sensor prototype to the integrated system.

architecture.title: Sense
architecture.text: MQ135 and MQ137 readings are combined with temperature, humidity, and camera-frame changes.

architecture.title: Interpret
architecture.text: Firmware filters readings, compares them with a clean-air baseline, and manages event state.

architecture.title: Record
architecture.text: Timestamped measurements and event photos are written to microSD with automatic recovery.

architecture.title: Present
architecture.text: The ESP32 serves a live dashboard, camera stream, and status feedback without a cloud dependency.

approach.title: Relative sensing
approach.text: The firmware reports changes from a startup baseline rather than claiming absolute ppm values. Temperature and humidity provide context for interpreting sensor drift.

approach.title: Local presence detection
approach.text: Camera-frame difference replaces cloud vision and, in later variants, the separate PIR sensor. New presence events can trigger locally stored images.

approach.title: Resilient field behavior
approach.text: The device retries failed storage operations, synchronizes timestamps, and falls back to its own Wi-Fi access point when the configured network is unavailable.

responsibilities: Implemented all embedded firmware and supporting Python utilities.
Built sensor acquisition, baseline calibration, filtering, and event-state logic.
Created camera presence detection, the embedded dashboard, networking, and microSD logging.
Wired and debugged the prototype and designed the ventilated 3D-printed enclosure.
verification: Validated six self-contained hardware configurations across dedicated branches.
Recorded timestamped readings, environmental deltas, and presence state to CSV.
Tested station Wi-Fi and local access-point operation for disconnected demonstrations.
Verified event-photo capture, storage recovery, and live dashboard updates on the final build.
limitations: Gas readings show relative change and are not calibrated safety, health, or veterinary measurements.
Camera sensitivity varies with lighting, placement, and threshold selection.
A production revision would replace breadboard wiring with a custom PCB and protected power inputs.

title: Thermal Presence TinyML System
summary: An end-to-end occupancy monitor that runs a quantized neural network locally on an ESP32-S3 and streams results to an authenticated dashboard.
role: Embedded ML and full-stack system development
focus: TinyML, MQTT, feature engineering, and IoT architecture
stack: ESP32-S3 · AMG8833 · TensorFlow Lite Micro · FastAPI · MQTT · MySQL · Docker
challenge: Detect human presence from a low-resolution 8x8 thermal sensor while keeping inference private, fast, and small enough for a microcontroller.
process: Engineered 76 spatial and statistical features, evaluated with group-aware validation, quantized the model, and exported the exact preprocessing pipeline to firmware.
outcome: Delivered local inference plus an authenticated, real-time dashboard with database storage and WebSocket updates.
overview: This project turns a 64-pixel thermal frame into a complete edge-AI product. The ESP32-S3 computes the same engineered features used during training, applies the exported scaler, and runs an INT8 neural network locally. Predictions and sensor frames travel through MQTT to a FastAPI service, where they are stored in MySQL and streamed to authenticated browsers in real time.

architecture.title: Capture
architecture.text: The AMG8833 supplies 64 thermal pixels plus an ambient thermistor reading.

architecture.title: Engineer
architecture.text: Firmware derives 76 normalized spatial, statistical, gradient, and hot-region features.

architecture.title: Infer
architecture.text: A 32-16-1 INT8 network predicts presence locally with TensorFlow Lite Micro.

architecture.title: Connect
architecture.text: MQTT, FastAPI, MySQL, WebSockets, and Canvas power the live authenticated dashboard.

approach.title: Feature parity
approach.text: Training and deployment share one 76-feature contract and the same StandardScaler values. Generated C++ headers carry the model and preprocessing parameters into firmware.

approach.title: Group-aware evaluation
approach.text: A held-out GroupKFold partition prevents readings from the same collection participant appearing in both training and evaluation.

approach.title: End-to-end delivery
approach.text: The system covers collection validation and backup, embedded inference, MQTT commands, persistence, authentication, WebSocket updates, and an 8x8 browser heatmap.

responsibilities: Developed thermal-frame normalization and spatial/statistical feature extraction.
Built data validation, retry, local backup, and class-balance tooling.
Implemented group-isolated training, scaling, INT8 export, and Python-to-C++ artifact generation.
Created ESP32 inference, MQTT messaging, FastAPI services, MySQL persistence, and the live dashboard.
verification: Measured 89.04% accuracy on 3,513 readings held out by collection group.
Recorded 88.97% empty-room F1 and 89.12% person-present F1 across 101 groups.
Added tests for collection validation, TinyML artifacts, preprocessing parity, and API behavior.
GitHub Actions runs Python tests and a complete ESP32 firmware build.
limitations: The source dataset is private because it contains participant identifiers.
A private authenticated MQTT broker is required for sensitive deployment.
Accuracy depends on sensor position, room geometry, and training-data coverage.

title: Renewable Energy MPPT Control
alt: Simulated solar MPPT power response converging to the maximum power point
summary: Solar and wind energy conversion systems using interleaved converters, closed-loop control, and maximum power point tracking.
focus: Converters, PI control, MPPT, and simulation
stack: Altair PSIM · P&O MPPT · Buck-boost converter · PWM
challenge: Maintain maximum energy extraction across changing source conditions while controlling a multi-leg converter and battery interface.
process: Characterized source behavior, tuned inner current and outer voltage loops, implemented perturb-and-observe tracking, and verified transient response.
outcome: Reached approximately 2,249 W from a 2,250 W theoretical solar maximum and demonstrated wind-system adaptation across multiple speeds.
overview: The work spans two PSIM studies: a 600 V photovoltaic source charging a 100 V battery, and a variable-speed wind turbine coupled to a permanent-magnet generator. Both systems use three-leg interleaved buck-boost conversion and layered feedback control, then add perturb-and-observe tracking to follow the source's maximum-power operating point.

architecture.title: Characterize
architecture.text: Source curves establish target voltage or shaft-speed regions for each operating condition.

architecture.title: Regulate
architecture.text: Inner current loops and outer voltage or speed loops stabilize converter behavior.

architecture.title: Track
architecture.text: Perturb-and-observe logic adjusts the reference using measured power response.

architecture.title: Convert
architecture.text: Three 120-degree interleaved buck-boost legs transfer energy to the 100 V battery.

approach.title: Solar conversion
approach.text: An outer PV-voltage controller generates the reference for three current-controlled legs. The system converges near 449 V and 5 A, approximately 1.3 W below the theoretical maximum.

approach.title: Wind conversion
approach.text: Turbine power-speed curves define optimum shaft speeds. A PI speed loop drives converter current while a C-block MPPT controller updates the reference.

approach.title: Interleaved control
approach.text: Three converter phases use 120-degree-shifted 10 kHz PWM and 400 uH inductors to share current and reduce aggregate ripple.

responsibilities: Built and validated the solar converter current-control and PV-voltage loops.
Integrated the three phase-shifted converter legs.
Characterized generator behavior and turbine power curves.
Designed the wind-system MPPT algorithm and analyzed both systems' simulation results.
verification: Solar output reached 2,248.7-2,249.9 W against a 2,250 W theoretical maximum.
Wind maximum-power points measured 5.63, 19.00, and 45.05 kW at 8, 12, and 16 m/s.
The wind system reached its initial 12 m/s operating region in 0.073 seconds.
A 12 m/s to 8 m/s transition settled in approximately 0.049 seconds.
limitations: Reported values are simulation results rather than physical converter measurements.
Solver, sampling, and switching settings can create small numerical differences.
Hardware deployment would require component-loss, protection, sensing, and gate-drive design.

title: FPGA Viterbi Decoder
summary: A synthesizable rate-1/2 convolutional encoder and eight-state hard-decision Viterbi decoder with self-checking verification.
focus: Digital communications, FPGA architecture, and error experiments
challenge: Implement add-compare-select path metrics and survivor traceback as deterministic, synthesizable hardware.
process: Built a reference model, parameterized the RTL, generated reproducible channel errors, and verified decoded output after pipeline latency.
outcome: Completed synthesis and fitting for Cyclone V with portable model tests and structured experiment documentation.
overview: This project implements the complete digital link around a rate-1/2, constraint-length-4 convolutional code. The transmitter generates two coded bits for every input bit; the receiver scores legal trellis transitions, updates eight path metrics, stores survivor decisions, and traces back through 64 symbols to recover the most likely data stream.

architecture.title: Encode
architecture.text: A constraint-length-4 convolutional encoder emits a rate-1/2 coded stream.

architecture.title: Disturb
architecture.text: Deterministic, seeded-random, fixed, and burst errors model channel corruption.

architecture.title: Score
architecture.text: Hamming branch metrics feed add-compare-select updates for all eight states.

architecture.title: Recover
architecture.text: Stored survivor choices drive 64-symbol traceback and delayed output comparison.

approach.title: Reference before RTL
approach.text: An executable Python model provides a portable behavioral reference for the encoder, trellis, path metrics, and error cases before hardware simulation.

approach.title: Parameterized decoder
approach.text: The SystemVerilog design consolidates branch metrics, ACS updates, survivor memory, and traceback into a synthesizable decoder.

approach.title: Reproducible channel study
approach.text: Experiments cover evenly spaced, seeded-random, and consecutive burst errors on either or both channel bits.

responsibilities: Implemented the encoder and Viterbi decoder datapaths in SystemVerilog.
Integrated the error channel and latency-aware comparison path.
Created the error experiments, self-checking testbench, and Python reference model.
Ran Quartus synthesis and fitting and analyzed fixed, random, and burst-error behavior.
verification: The RTL testbench generates 512 deterministic pseudo-random source bits.
Decoded output is checked automatically after the configured traceback latency.
Portable Python unit tests exercise the model independently of commercial FPGA tools.
Cyclone V synthesis and fitting completed with 559 ALMs and 579 registers.
limitations: The decoder uses hard-decision Hamming metrics rather than soft-decision confidence values.
The 64-symbol traceback introduces deterministic decoding latency.
Archived timing constraints require further optimization; timing closure is not claimed.

title: CPU Performance Engineering
summary: A measured study of compiler optimization, processor pipelines, memory hierarchy, cache locality, and multithreaded contention.
focus: C++, x86, caches, TLBs, OpenMP, and performance counters
stack: C++ · OpenMP · x86 assembly · Jupyter · GitHub Actions
challenge: Explain why source-level complexity and thread count often fail to predict real execution time.
process: Connected wall-clock measurements to instruction count, CPI, cache behavior, branch prediction, false sharing, and Amdahl's Law.
outcome: Created a privacy-safe, tested engineering report with standalone demonstrations and machine-readable measurements.
overview: Five processor experiments were consolidated into a focused study of where execution time actually goes. Instead of treating optimization as a single compiler switch, the project connects source structure to generated instructions, pipeline behavior, cache and TLB locality, coherence traffic, synchronization, and the limits of parallel scaling.

architecture.title: Measure
architecture.text: Collect wall time and hardware-counter evidence under controlled benchmark variants.

architecture.title: Locate
architecture.text: Separate instruction-count, CPI, cache, branch, TLB, and synchronization effects.

architecture.title: Change
architecture.text: Modify optimization level, data layout, traversal order, affinity, or sharing strategy.

architecture.title: Explain
architecture.text: Relate the observed ratio to the CPU performance equation and Amdahl's Law.

approach.title: From code to cycles
approach.text: Compiler and x86 studies connect code changes to instruction count, CPI, branch behavior, instruction-level parallelism, and critical-path limits.

approach.title: Memory hierarchy
approach.text: Traversal, stride, padding, working-set, and loop-order experiments reveal when cache, TLB, and prefetching dominate nominal complexity.

approach.title: Parallelism under pressure
approach.text: False sharing, affinity, locks, shared histograms, and private reductions show when coherence and contention exceed useful work.

responsibilities: Ran the processor, memory, and multithreading experiments.
Interpreted performance counters and performed CPI, latency, and speedup calculations.
Compared compiler, locality, data-layout, and synchronization strategies.
Produced privacy-safe reports, standalone C++ demonstrations, and machine-readable results.
verification: Compiler optimization produced a measured 3.42x speedup.
Row-major traversal was 13.77x faster than column-major traversal.
Cache-aware loop ordering increased observed hit rate from 14.24% to 93.73%.
Measured hierarchy latency was approximately 5, 14, 26, and 100 cycles for L1, L2, L3, and memory.
limitations: Measurements come from the original course system and are hardware-specific.
Standalone programs demonstrate the mechanisms but do not reproduce every original result.
Repeated-run ratios are more meaningful than treating one absolute time as universal.

title: Digital Image Processing Toolkit
alt: Six image-processing results including filtering, edge detection, compression, and segmentation
summary: A tested Python toolkit spanning geometric transforms, Fourier filtering, restoration, compression, morphology, and segmentation.
focus: Classical computer vision and numerical computing
stack: Python · NumPy · SciPy · OpenCV · PyWavelets · pytest
challenge: Turn six course experiments into a reusable package without carrying over assignment scaffolding or private material.
process: Refactored algorithms into modules, corrected the Fourier round-trip result, added validation and deterministic controls, and built tests.
outcome: Published an installable toolkit with a visual demo and successful local and GitHub CI verification.
overview: The toolkit reorganizes six image-processing experiments into an installable Python package that exposes the underlying numerical ideas. Core operations are implemented with NumPy rather than hidden behind single-call library equivalents, keeping transformations, filtering, reconstruction, compression, morphology, edge detection, and clustering readable and testable.

architecture.title: Transform
architecture.text: Centered rotation and inverse mapping support nearest-neighbor and bilinear sampling.

architecture.title: Enhance
architecture.text: Histogram, Laplacian, Sobel, Fourier, and restoration operations reveal image structure.

architecture.title: Represent
architecture.text: DCT and multilevel wavelets explore the quality-cost tradeoff of coefficient removal.

architecture.title: Understand
architecture.text: Morphology, edge suppression, components, and k-means turn pixels into regions.

approach.title: Readable fundamentals
approach.text: Direct DFT/IDFT and conditional-dilation connected components remain as clear reference implementations so the math and iteration stay visible.

approach.title: Reproducible experiments
approach.text: Randomized k-means accepts a seed, demo generation is standalone, and validation covers shape, ranges, parameters, and edge cases.

approach.title: Portfolio refactor
approach.text: Notebook logic was consolidated, the Fourier round-trip output was corrected, and public APIs were grouped into reusable modules.

responsibilities: Implemented algorithms across all six original experiments.
Conducted, visualized, and interpreted the numerical studies.
Reorganized notebook implementations into a reusable Python package.
Added validation, deterministic controls, automated tests, and a standalone demo.
verification: Tests cover geometric transforms and numerical DFT/IDFT reconstruction.
Compression tests validate DCT and wavelet behavior under coefficient removal.
Vision tests exercise components, edge processing, and seeded segmentation.
The demo reproduces filtering, restoration, compression, morphology, and segmentation outputs.
limitations: Direct DFT and iterative references favor clarity over production-scale performance.
Thresholds and filter parameters remain image- and noise-dependent.
The toolkit is educational and does not replace optimized production libraries.

title: CMOS VLSI Design and Verification
alt: CMOS physical layout from a Cadence Virtuoso design
summary: Transistor-level digital IC design, timing characterization, layout, and physical verification in Cadence Virtuoso.
focus: CMOS logic, sequential circuits, DRC/LVS, timing, and power
stack: Cadence Virtuoso · HSPICE · CMOS · DRC · LVS
metric: DRC/LVS verified · 49.31 ps minimum passing period
challenge: Connect transistor sizing and logical effort to verified timing, power, and physical-layout results.
process: Designed gates and transmission-gate storage elements, constructed testbenches, swept timing constraints, and completed physical checks.
outcome: Documented a progression from static CMOS cells to a registered consecutive-ones detector with verification evidence.
overview: Three studies build from transistor-level static CMOS gates to sequential storage and a synchronous datapath. Each stage pairs schematic design with testbench construction and measurement: first logical-effort sizing and layout verification, then latch and flip-flop timing, and finally a registered consecutive-ones detector evaluated for function, period, and power.

architecture.title: Design
architecture.text: Transistor networks implement static logic, transmission-gate storage, and the detector datapath.

architecture.title: Size
architecture.text: Logical effort and load targets guide stage count and device sizing.

architecture.title: Simulate
architecture.text: HSPICE testbenches measure propagation, setup, hold, clock-to-Q, period, and power.

architecture.title: Verify
architecture.text: Cadence layout, DRC, LVS, waveforms, and vector sweeps connect intent to evidence.

approach.title: Static CMOS
approach.text: NAND, NOR, inverter, and buffer-chain designs establish sizing, logical effort, transition slope, average power, and physical verification.

approach.title: Sequential timing
approach.text: Transmission-gate latches and master-slave flip-flops are characterized for setup, hold, clock-to-Q, path delay, and minimum period.

approach.title: Integrated detector
approach.text: A four-input adjacent-ones detector is wrapped with registers for functional vectors, clock-period sweeps, and power analysis.

responsibilities: Designed the transistor-level logic, latch, flip-flop, and detector circuits.
Sized devices and stages using logical-effort reasoning.
Constructed testbenches and measured timing, power, and transitions.
Created physical layouts, ran DRC/LVS, and analyzed the critical path.
verification: Lab 1 completed design-rule and layout-versus-schematic checks.
Lab 2 measured 12.598 ps setup, -22.598 ps hold, and 20.254 ps maximum clock-to-Q.
The tested sequential path passed at a 49.31 ps minimum simulated period.
The detector reported a 68.8 ps period and 398.689 uW total simulated power.
limitations: Results are simulations from a licensed academic process environment, not fabricated silicon.
The original process-design kit and waveform databases cannot be redistributed.
Cleaned netlists require compatible device-model definitions to run.

title: House of Odds
alt: House of Odds probability learning game title screen
summary: A casino-themed probability-learning game with three acts, rewards, performance summaries, and automated testing.
focus: Interactive learning, application architecture, and quality assurance
stack: TypeScript · Vite · Konva · Prisma · SQLite · Vitest
challenge: Coordinate state, canvas interaction, persistent questions, rewards, and reliable navigation across a multi-stage game.
process: Continued the team project with preserved attribution, structured the application around models, controllers, and views, and expanded tests.
outcome: Delivered a playable learning experience with per-act accuracy, retry flows, database-backed content, and CI.
overview: House of Odds turns probability practice into a three-act casino journey. Questions, rewards, navigation, and the final performance report are coordinated across an MVC-inspired TypeScript architecture and rendered through Konva. This repository preserves the original team history while documenting and testing my final-results feature and integration work.

architecture.title: Persist
architecture.text: Prisma and SQLite provide the question data used by each act.

architecture.title: Model
architecture.text: Question, reward, act, and result models hold gameplay state and statistics.

architecture.title: Coordinate
architecture.text: Controllers and AppScreenSwitcher manage input, validation, rewards, and screen flow.

architecture.title: Render
architecture.text: Konva views draw the title, questions, rewards, and final results on a 1280 x 720 stage.

approach.title: Results as a feature
approach.text: The final-results model calculates correct and incorrect totals, overall accuracy, and a per-act breakdown, then resets the run cleanly.

approach.title: Screen-flow integration
approach.text: AppScreenSwitcher connects the title, three question acts, reward screens, and end state while controllers separate state changes from rendering.

approach.title: Acceptance-led testing
approach.text: Tests follow user-facing requirements: navigation reaches the intended screen, answers and rewards update correctly, and restarting begins cleanly.

responsibilities: Implemented the end-of-game model, controller, and Konva view.
Calculated overall and per-act correct, incorrect, and accuracy values.
Integrated the results screen and complete restart behavior.
Added regression tests and resolved merge, initialization, and CI issues.
verification: The repository contains 38 passing tests across eight files.
Tests cover state, controllers, title/results screens, navigation, and the database adapter.
Strict TypeScript checking and a Vite production build run with the test suite.
Manual testing exercised the final-question-to-results-to-restart flow.
limitations: The game targets a fixed 1280 x 720 canvas and is not yet responsive.
Question content currently uses a development SQLite database.
The automated suite is useful regression coverage but not full end-to-end testing.
